Backpressure is a flow-control signal by which a consumer that cannot keep up makes its producers slow down, buffer or shed load instead of overrunning it.

In a message queue it appears at three points: the broker bounds a queue and blocks or rejects publishers once it is full (publisher confirms make that visible to the producer); the consumer caps unacknowledged deliveries with a prefetch limit; and a pull-based consumer pauses fetching while its local buffer drains. The tradeoff is latency against loss: blocking publishers keeps every message but pushes delay upstream, while dropping or dead-lettering keeps latency flat and loses work.

Prefetch limits, bounded queues and pause/resume on the consumer are the usual mechanisms.
